explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, "…everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled." (Luke 18:31) The prophets were the ones holding the pen. Jesus is saying the whole trip to Jerusalem was written down long before anybody packed a bag.

Kings had plenty to say, friend, but that's not who Jesus names. He says, "…everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled." (Luke 18:31) So the answer is the prophets. The kings can keep their crowns, the writing job belongs to somebody else.

Scribes did a lot of writing, so I see why that looked tasty. But Jesus says, "…everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled." (Luke 18:31) The writers He points to are the prophets. He doesn't mention scribes at all.

explanations.answer: Mocked and insulted and spit upon
explanations.explanation: Right, and it's a heavy one. Jesus says, "He will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon." (Luke 18:32) The Gentiles are the people outside of Israel. I think this part hurts to hear, and Jesus says it plainly anyway.

explanations.answer: Welcomed and honored as a guest
explanations.explanation: I wish the card went that way, friend, but it doesn't. Jesus says the Son of Man "will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon." (Luke 18:32) No guest treatment here. It's a heavy verse, and the right answer is the mocking.

That one sounds a lot gentler than what Jesus says. He says, "He will be delivered over to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon." (Luke 18:32) Nothing about being set free in that verse. It's a heavy one, baker, so we just let it be heavy.

True! Jesus says, "They will flog Him and kill Him, and on the third day He will rise again." (Luke 18:33) The hard part comes first, but it isn't the last word. Rising again is the last thing He says in that sentence.

It's actually true, friend. Jesus says, "They will flog Him and kill Him, and on the third day He will rise again." (Luke 18:33) So the text does say the Son of Man will rise. The sentence ends with the rising, not with the flogging.

explanations.answer: The meaning was hidden from them
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says, "The meaning was hidden from them, and they did not comprehend what He was saying." (Luke 18:34) It doesn't tell us who hid it or why. So we leave it right where the text leaves it.

explanations.answer: He spoke to them in a parable
explanations.explanation: Nope, no parable in this one. Jesus speaks plainly about Jerusalem, the Gentiles and the third day. Then the text says, "The meaning was hidden from them, and they did not comprehend what He was saying." (Luke 18:34) The words were clear, but the meaning was hidden.

explanations.answer: They were too far away to hear
explanations.explanation: They were close, friend. Jesus "took the Twelve aside" and spoke to them (Luke 18:31). Hearing wasn't the trouble. The text says, "The meaning was hidden from them, and they did not comprehend what He was saying." (Luke 18:34)
That's the one. The text says the blind man "was sitting beside the road, begging." (Luke 18:35) He's sitting there asking people for help. That sets up everything he does next.
Weaving is a fine job, baker, but it's not in this verse. The text says the blind man "was sitting beside the road, begging." (Luke 18:35) No loom, no thread. Just a man by the road asking for help.
He does get loud later, so I see the thinking. But the text says he "was sitting beside the road, begging." (Luke 18:35) Begging is the word. The shouting comes when he hears who's passing by.

explanations.answer: Jesus of Nazareth is passing by
explanations.explanation: Yes! "Jesus of Nazareth is passing by," they told him. (Luke 18:37) He can't see the crowd, but he can hear it, and now he knows who's in it. Watch what he does with that news.
No governor in this crowd, friend. The people tell him, "Jesus of Nazareth is passing by." (Luke 18:37) That's the news the blind man gets. And he does not waste it.

explanations.answer: A wedding party is passing by
explanations.explanation: That would be a lot of noise for a good reason, but it's not what the crowd says. They tell him, "Jesus of Nazareth is passing by." (Luke 18:37) So the commotion is about Jesus, baker.

Right, baker. He calls out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" (Luke 18:38) He sits there begging, yet the thing he asks Jesus for is mercy. Son of David is a title for the promised King, so he's calling Jesus by a big name.
I see why, since the man is a beggar. But he calls out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" (Luke 18:38) The word is mercy. Money never comes up in what he says to Jesus.
A guide would make sense for a blind man, friend. But the text has him cry out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" (Luke 18:38) He asks for mercy. He doesn't ask for a guide.

Not quite, baker. The text says the people at the front "admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”" (Luke 18:39) So he doesn't go quiet. He gets louder.

False is right! The people leading the way "admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”" (Luke 18:39) Somebody says hush, and he turns the volume UP. I could never do that. I'd fold like a cookie box in the rain.

explanations.answer: Stops and has him brought over
explanations.explanation: That's right. "Jesus stopped and directed that the man be brought to Him." (Luke 18:40) The crowd was busy telling the man to be quiet, and Jesus stops the whole walk. He wants this man brought to Him.

explanations.answer: Sends the crowd to quiet him
explanations.explanation: The crowd tries that on its own, but Jesus doesn't. The text says, "Jesus stopped and directed that the man be brought to Him." (Luke 18:40) He doesn't send anybody to hush the man. He sends for him.

explanations.answer: Calls back to him and keeps walking
explanations.explanation: Close on the calling, friend, but Jesus doesn't keep walking. The text says, "Jesus stopped and directed that the man be brought to Him." (Luke 18:40) He stops, and the man is brought over.

explanations.answer: What do you want Me to do for you
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus asks him, "What do you want Me to do for you?" (Luke 18:41) The man had been calling for mercy, and now Jesus asks him straight out. The man gets to say it in his own words.

explanations.answer: Why are you shouting at Me
explanations.explanation: The man was loud, I'll give you that. But Jesus doesn't scold him. He asks, "What do you want Me to do for you?" (Luke 18:41) That's a question that invites the man to answer.
Good guess, since the crowd had just told the man who was passing. But that's not what Jesus asks. He says, "What do you want Me to do for you?" (Luke 18:41)
True, baker. Jesus says, "Receive your sight!" and then, "Your faith has healed you." (Luke 18:42) Those are His exact words to the man. And the man had been crying out to Jesus the whole time.
It's actually true, friend. Jesus tells him, "Receive your sight!" and then, "Your faith has healed you." (Luke 18:42) So yes, Jesus says that to the man near Jericho.

explanations.answer: Follows Jesus and gives God the glory
explanations.explanation: That's it! The man "received his sight and followed Jesus, glorifying God." (Luke 18:43) The first thing he does with his new eyes is follow Jesus. And he's giving God the glory while he does it.

explanations.answer: Goes home and tells his family
explanations.explanation: Going home would be a nice thing to do, but the text doesn't say it. It says he "received his sight and followed Jesus, glorifying God." (Luke 18:43) He follows Jesus. Family doesn't come up.

explanations.answer: Runs into Jericho to tell the town
explanations.explanation: Plenty of people would sprint off with news like that, friend. But the text says he "received his sight and followed Jesus, glorifying God." (Luke 18:43) He follows Jesus. Nothing about running into town.

True! The text says, "And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God." (Luke 18:43) The man isn't the only one praising. Everybody who saw it joins in, even the crowd that was telling him to hush.
It's actually true, baker. Luke 18:43 says, "And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God." So the crowd joins the praise. That's a long way from "be silent."
